title: Data Manipulation
summary: Data Manipulation covers adversary changes to information that affect what a person, process or system concludes from it. The goal is not to steal the data or make it unavailable, but to make it wrong in a way that serves the attacker, whether that shifts a business outcome, misleads analysts or covers the traces of other activity. The technique spans stored records, data moving between systems, and data that exists only in memory, and the practical impact depends entirely on which process consumes it. Because the visible symptom is a wrong number or a missing row rather than a broken service, the failure usually surfaces through business reconciliation, comparison with a source of truth or an integrity check rather than through an availability alert. Meaningful manipulation of a complex system generally requires knowledge of that system's data model, so unusual interest in schemas, reports and query patterns is relevant context for defenders.

beginner.definition: Data is the information that a system keeps and uses. Data manipulation means changing that information on purpose. An attacker might add a record, remove one, or alter a value. The system keeps working normally, but the information it shows is no longer true.
beginner.whyItMatters: A broken system is easy to notice, because nothing works. Wrong data is much harder to see. Staff may make decisions based on numbers that an attacker changed. Records may be deleted so that other activity stays hidden. Money, safety and trust can all be affected. Because everything still runs, this kind of attack can continue for a long time.
howItWorks: The attacker first learns how the target system stores and uses its data.
They then add, change or delete records where the system keeps its information.
One goal is to change an outcome, such as a payment amount or a stock level.
Another goal is to hide evidence, for example by removing log or audit entries.
Because the application still runs, users may not notice that results are wrong.
The wrong data then spreads into reports, decisions and other connected systems.
beginner.example: Imagine a warehouse where every box is written into a ledger by hand. The shelves stay tidy and the forklift keeps working, so nothing looks broken. One night a worker changes a few numbers in the ledger instead of moving any boxes. The next morning the manager reads that ten items are in stock when only three are there. Orders go out, customers are promised goods that do not exist, and the mistake spreads to invoices. Data manipulation is that changed ledger. The warehouse is fine, but the records lie.
takeaways: Attacks on data are quiet, because the system still appears to work.
Compare important records with a trusted source to spot changes.
Not every attack breaks a system; some attacks change its answers.

objectives: Define data manipulation and explain how it differs from data theft or destruction.
Describe the goals an attacker may have when changing data in a system.
Explain why this behaviour is difficult to detect using system health alerts alone.
Identify the records and comparisons that can reveal altered data.
Explain why knowledge of a target system's data model matters to an attacker.
